decisions.final:
Step 1, the Loss Component. The Loss Component is 15 times average annual operational risk losses incurred over the previous ten years:

$$LC = 15 \times 0.200 = \text{EUR } 3.00 \text{ billion}$$

Step 2, the ratio.

$$\frac{LC}{BIC} = \frac{3.00}{2.67} = 1.1236$$

Because LC exceeds BIC, the ILM must be greater than one before any arithmetic is done: a bank with losses that are high relative to its BIC is required to hold higher capital.

Step 3, the Internal Loss Multiplier.

$$ILM = \ln\left[e - 1 + \frac{LC}{BIC}\right] = \ln[2.71828 - 1 + 1.1236] = \ln[2.84188] = 1.0445$$

Formula version note. The BCBS December 2017 text (the Ch. 24 reading) raises the ratio to the power 0.8: $ILM = \ln\left[e - 1 + (LC/BIC)^{0.8}\right]$. With the exponent, $(1.1236)^{0.8} = 1.0977$, $ILM = \ln[2.8160] = 1.0353$ and $ORC = 2.67 \times 1.0353 = \text{EUR } 2.76$ billion, which is still nearest to (c) EUR 2.79 billion. The plain-ratio form used in this question gives 1.0445 and EUR 2.79 billion.

Step 4, the capital charge.

$$ORC = BIC \times ILM = 2.67 \times 1.0445 = \text{EUR } 2.7889 \text{ billion, or nearest EUR } 2.79 \text{ billion}$$

Behavioural check. The formula is constructed so that:

$$LC = BIC \implies \frac{LC}{BIC} = 1 \implies ILM = \ln[e] = 1$$
$$LC > BIC \implies ILM > 1 \implies \text{higher capital}$$
$$LC < BIC \implies ILM < 1 \implies \text{lower capital}$$

Two framework qualifications matter. Banks with fewer than five years of high-quality loss data must calculate the requirement solely on the Business Indicator Component, and banks that fail the loss data standards must hold capital at a minimum equal to 100% of the BIC, with supervisors able to require an ILM greater than one. Separately, the ILM has been left to national discretion, so a supervisor may set it equal to one for all banks in the jurisdiction, in which case ORC simply equals BIC. The stem rules that discretion out.
decisions.reason: Source PDF p.32 uses ILM = ln[e-1+LC/BIC] (plain ratio); BCBS d424 OPE text has (LC/BIC)^0.8, as do the repo notes (12_OR_ORR24.tex l.74). Recomputed: plain ILM 1.04446, ORC 2.7887; ^0.8 ILM 1.03531, ORC 2.7643. Both nearest to (c) 2.79 (next option 2.67 is 0.094 away). Key (c) stands; the note prevents a BCBS-trained candidate from doubting the key. Distractor (a) still maps to the dropped-15 error under both forms (1.559 / 1.634).

decisions.final: (d) is an intermediate-result trap with a second route into it: the Loss Component is a legitimate intermediate quantity, and the naive multiplier of LC divided by BIC arrives at the same figure, which makes the option doubly attractive. The logarithm exists precisely to damp the adjustment, so a bank whose losses run 12% above its BIC faces a capital uplift of about 4.5% (about 3.5% under the BCBS form with the 0.8 exponent), not 12%. (a) is a dropped term, omitting the multiple of 15. (b) is a wrong input twin, substituting the BIC for the ORC by assuming the ILM equals one; note the stem plants the national discretion sentence specifically to test whether you read it. A useful sanity check before computing: establish the direction from the LC versus BIC comparison first, then verify that your arithmetic moves the capital the same way.
decisions.reason: Companion to the solution note: uplift is 4.45% under the plain form and 3.53% under the ^0.8 form (python check). Wording slightly changed from auditor's proposal for clarity; substance identical.

decisions.final:
$$ORC = BIC \times ILM$$
$$BIC = \text{Business Indicator Component} = BI \times \text{marginal coefficients } (12\%, 15\%, 18\% \text{ by bucket})$$
$$ILM = \text{Internal Loss Multiplier} = \ln\left[e - 1 + \frac{LC}{BIC}\right]$$
$$LC = \text{Loss Component} = 15 \times \text{average annual operational risk losses over the previous 10 years}$$
$$RWA_{\text{operational risk}} = 12.5 \times ORC$$

Formula version note: the BCBS December 2017 text raises the ratio to the power 0.8, $ILM = \ln\left[e - 1 + (LC/BIC)^{0.8}\right]$; some curriculum summaries show it without the exponent. The structure (BIC as the base, ILM as the multiplier) is the same either way, so the key is unaffected.

The business figure is the base and the loss figure is the multiplier. The ten-year loss history enters the calculation through the ILM, not as the base of the capital charge. The escalation of the coefficients with size reflects the regulatory judgement that operational risk grows more than proportionally with size, because the larger the organisation the more complex its processes, operations and interactions.

decisions.final: The three lines of defence model has existed in some variation for over thirty years and gained visibility when the Institute of Internal Auditors published its position paper on the model, updated in 2020 as the IIA's Three Lines Model. In regard to the model, each of the following is true EXCEPT which one?
decisions.reason: The IIA published 'The IIA's Three Lines Model: An update of the Three Lines of Defense' in July 2020. Source PDF p.9 says 2021 (source error). Key (a) unaffected.

decisions.final: True, so not the answer. This is the substance of the 2020 IIA update: the second line is management, not a quasi-audit function.

decisions.final: (a) is a role misassignment in its first half and a polarity flip in its second, and both halves are wrong, which paradoxically makes the option easier to miss: a candidate who spots that the first line does not set appetite may hesitate over whether the culture clause rescues it. Option (c) is the strongest competing candidate, because a candidate who learned the older and more adversarial framing of the second line as pure independent challenge will read "provides support" as a contamination of independence. The 2020 update specifically reinstates expertise and support as second line roles and confines the challenge to risk-related matters.

added.proposed:
Statement (c) is false and inverts the central design feature of the new approach. Internal loss experience is retained, and it enters the calculation through the Internal Loss Multiplier:

$$ORC = BIC \times ILM, \qquad ILM = \ln\left[e - 1 + \frac{LC}{BIC}\right], \qquad LC = 15 \times \text{average annual operational risk losses over the previous 10 years}$$

(The BCBS text writes the ratio inside the ILM as $(LC/BIC)^{0.8}$; some curriculum summaries omit the exponent. Either way the ILM carries the bank's loss experience into the capital charge.)

A bank's internal operational risk loss experience therefore affects the calculation of operational risk capital directly. A bank with losses that are high relative to its BIC is required to hold higher capital, and conversely a bank with low losses relative to its BIC holds lower capital.

What the reform did eliminate is the internal model, not the internal loss data. Statement (b) states this correctly: the standardised approach for measuring minimum operational risk capital requirements replaces all existing approaches in the Basel II framework, that is BIA, TSA and AMA are all superseded by a single approach applying to internationally active banks on a consolidated basis, with supervisors retaining discretion to apply it to non-internationally active banks.

Two qualifications on the loss input are worth holding, because they are the nearest true statements to the false one in (c). Banks in bucket 1, with a BI at or below EUR 1 billion, have their ILM set to one, so internal loss data does not affect their capital calculation. And the ILM has been left to national discretion, so a supervisor may set it equal to one for all banks in the jurisdiction. Neither of those is the same as eliminating loss experience from the framework.
